title: Someone used Claude Code to build a Linux phone OS, and you can try it in your browser
excerpt: Dusty PinePhone reborn as a speedy feature device with 66 fps display rendering, modular apps on microSD and a WebAssembly demo.
content_html:
Published Nov 12, 2026, 6:56 AM EST

Hamed holds a B.A. in English Literature, and graduated top of his class. He loves music, tech gadgets, and exploring the latest in the world of LLMs. He also enjoys tinkering with creative software such as Logic Pro, Final Cut Pro, and Photoshop.

A lifelong musician, Hamed plays multiple instruments, including guitar, bass, and oud. He is equally fascinated by smart-home technology and can happily spend hours geeking out over connected lights, speakers, sensors, and automations that make everyday life a little more interesting. When he isn’t covering the latest tech news, he explores more creative topics on his Medium blog, works on his music, or clears his head by riding his motorcycle.

Summary

  • Claude Code rebuilt the original PinePhone firmware from kernel up, making it a fast feature phone.
  • Buildroot, patched Linux and LVGL drive a 66 FPS UI with quick boots and core apps like Telegram and Doom.
  • You can try the WebAssembly demo or boot the firmware from a microSD.

Remember the PinePhone? Someone took the seven-year-old Linux-based smartphone out of their drawer and used Claude Code to create new firmware for it from the kernel up. According to the creator's post on Reddit, embedded developer Elian Doran bought the phone a couple of years ago and left it collecting dust because of how slow it was. His answer was to turn it into a feature phone that boots in seconds and handles a handful of everyday tasks much more quickly.

The open-source firmware runs only on the original PinePhone, although Doran says he's thinking of porting it to the PinePhone Pro as well. He also built a browser demo that allows you to interact with the interface without installing the operating system.

How Claude Code helped make the PinePhone faster

Using Buildroot and a patched mainline Linux kernel, the creator built an interface that uses the LVGL graphics library to draw directly to the display. Doran says most screens run at the display's full 66 frames per second. Of the 81 patches in the project, 46 were for Linux itself that cover things like charging, camera support, and waking the phone when a text message arrives.

Doran admits that writing the C code itself was rarely the hard part. The tedious part of the project was tracing drivers and logs to find where to make changes. Thankfully, that's where Claude's agents can come in very handy. Doran relied on Opus 5.5 for most of the work and turned to Claude's recent Fable 5.2 for more complex problems such as debugging calls over 4G.

The project took nine days to develop, and Doran tallied 2,290 messages he typed across 187 Claude sessions. In a reply, Doran reported roughly 5 billion tokens, 93% of them cache reads, and said Claude generated 16.8 million output tokens. He estimated that the whole project would have cost about $1,750 at API rates.

Try the new PinePhone interface in your browser

You can navigate to the project's website and click "Try it live" to load the same interface compiled to WebAssembly. The demo simulates the phone's hardware, so you can't use the camera and calls ring silently. Moreover, the demo comes with some stock ebooks, photos, and music to try. The firmware on the physical phone supports separately installable apps, including a Telegram client, Doom, and a Sega Genesis emulator.

If you have an original PinePhone sitting around somewhere and want to test this out, you can boot the firmware from a microSD card. To switch back to your existing system, turn the phone off, remove the card, and turn it back on.
